items.title: A mole of marshmallows would cover the USA 600 miles deep
items.claim: 6.022 times 10 to the 23 is just a number until you try to picture it. Avogadro's number of marshmallows would bury the entire surface of the United States to a depth of 600 miles.
items.prompt: Roughly how many moles of water molecules are in a single drop (about 0.05 mL)?

options.text: About 0.003 moles, which is roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules
Around 6 times 10 to the 23 — one drop is one mole
About 0.05 moles, the same as the volume in millilitres

items.reveal_title: Even a microscopic drop contains stupefying numbers of molecules
items.reveal:
0.05 mL of water has a mass of 0.05 g. Water is 18 g per mole, so 0.05 / 18 equals about 0.0028 mol. Multiply by Avogadro's number and you get roughly 1.7 times 10 to the 21 molecules.

If you counted those molecules at one per second, it would take about 50 trillion years — over 3000 times the age of the universe. Chemistry is the study of mind-bending counts of incredibly tiny things.
items.why: The mole is treated as a unit conversion when it should be treated as a stark statement about scale.

items.title: Mean bond enthalpies are wrong for the molecule in front of you
items.claim: Look up the C-H bond enthalpy: 412 kJ/mol. Use it to predict the energy to break the first C-H in methane. You will be wrong. Use it for the fourth C-H — you will be wrong again, but in the opposite direction.

options.text: The energy to break any single C-H bond, exactly
The MEAN energy to break a C-H bond over many molecules and many environments — individual bond energies for CH4, CH3, CH2, CH range from about 339 to 439 kJ/mol
The energy to make a C-H bond, not break it
The energy to break a C-H bond at 0 kelvin

items.reveal_title: Successive bond dissociation differs from the average
items.reveal:
Break one C-H in methane: 439 kJ/mol (to form CH3 radical + H).
Break the next C-H in CH3: 461 kJ/mol.
The next in CH2: 424 kJ/mol.
The last in CH: 339 kJ/mol.

Mean: about 416 kJ/mol — close to the tabulated value, but no individual bond requires exactly that. The values differ because each radical intermediate has different stability.

Bond enthalpy calculations of reaction energies are approximations that get within about 30 kJ/mol of reality — useful for trends, dangerous for precise predictions. Hess's law with measured enthalpies of formation is more accurate.
items.why: Single tabulated values look authoritative. They are weighted averages, and the value for any specific bond can be very different.

items.title: Doubling the nucleophile can do nothing
items.claim: Double the concentration of OH- in some nucleophilic substitutions and the rate doubles. In others, the rate doesn't change at all. Same reactants, same nucleophile, very different kinetics.
items.prompt: What controls whether the reaction is SN1 or SN2?

options.text: The structure of the substrate — tertiary halides go via a carbocation intermediate (SN1, rate-determining step doesn't involve nucleophile), primary halides go via concerted backside attack (SN2, rate depends on nucleophile)
The solvent — only polar solvents allow SN2
The atomic number of the halide

items.reveal_title: Mechanism is destiny — and rate law reveals mechanism
items.reveal:
Tertiary carbon centres are sterically blocked from backside SN2 attack but they form stable tertiary carbocations on dissociation. So they go SN1: slow ionisation followed by fast nucleophilic capture. The rate law is first order — only in the substrate.

Primary carbon centres can't make a stable carbocation but they're sterically open. They go SN2: concerted, one-step, with inversion of configuration. Rate law is second order: rate proportional to [substrate][nucleophile].

The same product (an alcohol from a halide) hides two completely different mechanisms with different stereochemistry: racemisation (SN1) versus inversion (SN2).
items.why: Rate laws are not just empirical — they are direct readouts of which mechanism is at work.
